The tips stand the test of time and are especially relevant to attorneys and firm mangers trying to address the challenges created by recent economic fallout . Tip # NUM - Focus on Revenue When we face flat or even declining revenues , we often immediately look to expenses to offset the lost income . Itâ € ™ s always smart to keep an eye on expenses . In the words of another forefather , Ben Franklin , â € œBeware of little expenses ; a small leak will sink a great ship.â € ? However , this needs to be everyday diligence , not a knee-jerk reaction . Cuts made too deeply or too quickly can have long-term negative consequences . Reducing your marketing costs or reducing staff may result in the work not coming through the door or the ability to handle it when it does . Tip # NUM - Create a Budget How can you know where you are going unless you know where you have been ? And how do you respond to a change in conditions unless you know how it relates to your current situation ? By taking the time to analyze the data needed to create a budget , you will gain valuable insight into the sources of your income and expenses . Once in place , your budget can help you to identify changes in your practice , such as a decline in revenue , and can facilitate informed adjustments ( keeping Tip # NUM in mind ) . Tip # NUM - Develop a Financial Dashboard Suppose your Porsche came without a dashboard and speed odometer ; unless Lady Luck is on your side , at some point in time you would find yourself in trouble . The same may hold true for your practice or firm , especially in a challenging economy . Many of the practice management software titles are now equipped with dashboards . If your software does not offer such a tool , itâ € ™ s not as hard as you may believe to create a custom dashboard using data from your systems and Microsoft Excel . Tip # NUM - Record Your Time and Bill Your Clients I recently passed the NUM year mark and had to have a certain medical procedure performed . I knew that the procedure was for my own good and could ultimately save my life if there was something going on of which I was unaware.Ã ‚ As unpleasant as I thought it might be , I knew to put it off might be to my own peril . The same is true for recording time and billing clients . There is likely no better way to negatively impact cash flow than to not record time on a contemporaneous basis and to delay billing . Tip # NUM - Collect Your Money Having worked in the private sector , I can attest to the fact that attorneys are often the last ones in line to be paid . I believe that this is partly due to the fact that attorneys have passively trained their clients to behave in such a manner . If a controller or CFO knows that their attorney will never call to collect their fees , he or she will happily delay payment for the sake of cash flow . I recently read a study that showed that the likelihood of collecting fee receivables over NUM days is a mere NUM % . Once you bill your time , stay in touch with your clients . If NUM days seems too aggressive , set a higher threshold . But keep in mind that the older the receivable , the less likely you are to collect . This process is indeed time consuming , but well worth the investment . Should you truly not have the time , you may want to consider outsourcing your collection effort . In the midst of the engagement , keep your eye on the balance of the clientâ € ™ s retainer and strongly consider replenishing the balance if it has been depleted by progress billings . Just because the client has paid you once doesnâ € ™ t mean that they will pay you again . You may find yourself in the same frustrating position as the aforementioned Accounts Receivable Manager , negotiating a payment plan for dollars you expected to immediately collect . Tip # NUM - Over Communicate Although communication on its own was not a tip shared by the programâ € ™ s faculty , it was at the base of many . In all aspects of life , poor communication leads to misunderstanding , frustration and damaged relationships . We have all seen the damage caused by what Cool Hand Luke so aptly described as â € œa failure to communicate.â € ? Communicating undeniably takes an investment of time . But the consequences of not communicating can range from collection problems to a loss of clients . Why not make the investment up front ? The filing of the Articles of Dissolution places the corporate entity in a period of winding up and liquidating that continues until the Articles of Termination of corporate existence are filed ( See Section NUM . ) This procedure is outlined in the enclosed e-mail . There is no particular rush in accomplishing that step and there can be a disadvantage in doing so too early if there are accounts receivable remaining to be collected or if there are claims to be asserted against NUM parties . The only disadvantage to leaving this period open is that you must maintain an agent for service of process during that period . " . There is no legal requirement to do this and it is unusual in our regular corporate practice to do so . There are a number of reasons why we generally do not follow this section . NUM , most of our corporate clients ( including Driver 's Way ) intend to pay all the creditors of the dissolved entity , so there is no concern regarding unpaid bills that may come due later . Secondly , newspaper publication brings unwanted publicity and may encourage potential claimants ( encouraged by lawyers who regularly review the newspapers for claims ) to come forward . NUM , the benefit provided by the section ( a cutting off of claims after NUM years ) is not a worthwhile benefit because other statutes accomplish the same result . The principal benefit of the Section is that all claims against the corporation are cut off after a NUM period . If you pay all you claims , this makes no difference because they are satisfied in full and not subject to claim . If there are claims that are either ( i ) disputed or ( ii ) unknown , this Section might provide some benefit . In other words , the basic statute of limitations is actually shorter than the benefit provided by the notice provision . This is true with most of the types of claims that might be asserted by customers against Driver 's Way . As to other claims , there are a variety of reasons why your risk is low . NUM , we have incorporated arbitration clauses into the retail buyers orders of all AII entities , which means that customers are not able to sue us in court but must proceed with an informal arbitration procedure which rarely results in a huge benefit to the customer . Secondly , we have insurance for many types of liability . Thirdly , it has already been NUM years since the last car was sold by Driver 's Way , which means that the likelihood of any claim being asserted at this point is very remote . There may be cases in which it is appropriate or even important to publish notice of dissolution and obtain the benefit of the NUM period , but we are not aware of any circumstances with Driver 's Way which would suggest that course of action . < URL > < URL > SC Supreme Court Refuses to Protect the Lender in Another UPL Case Once again the South Carolina Supreme Court has held a lender 's feet to the fire for failing to comply with the state 's strict unauthorized practice of law rulings . Matrix Financial Services refinanced its own loan , using a non-attorney service provider to conduct a title search , prepare loan documents and close the refinanced loan . The mortgage for the refinance was recorded after an intervening judgment was domesticated in South Carolina . That intervening judgment lienholder sought to assert its priority in the foreclosure by Matrix . Matrix asked the court apply the doctrine of equitable subrogation to put it back in its priority position prior to the refinance . The Master-in-Equity did so , but the SC Supreme Court reversed the decision , refusing to allow the equitable subrogation on several grounds , including unclean hands . The Court denied relief , in part , because it found that Matrix had committed the unauthorized practice of law in closing the refinance mortgage , " clearly violating South Carolina law . " The Court concluded that " a party can not violate the law and expect not to bear the consequences of its actions . " Our thanks to Sharon Bramlett of the McNair Firm , our South Carolina State Editor , for bringing this case to our attention . As Sharon points out , " our appellate courts are on a roll and are sending a strong message they are not backing down on the issue of UPL .
